claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, unoptimized surface oxide layer.
Pre-treatment annealing of Q235 steel induces a coherent and adherent oxide scale.
The annealing-induced oxide scale significantly reduces high-temperature salt-induced corrosion degradation relative to as-received Q235 steel.
Annealing has less effect on corrosion protection at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
A coherent, adherent, and dense oxide scale acts as a barrier to ion diffusion and chemical attack.
Annealing facilitates controlled oxidation of Q235 steel.
Controlled oxidation during annealing produces a well-adhered and uniform oxide layer.
At high temperature, the annealing-induced oxide scale impedes ingress of corrosive species from the salt environment.
Impeded ingress of corrosive species limits corrosion degradation.
Slow room-temperature corrosion kinetics make the difference between annealed and untreated Q235 steel minimal.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will show lower mass change than untreated steel.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will show fewer and shallower corrosion pits than untreated steel.
The protective benefit is expected to apply specifically under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
If the as-received oxide layer is already structurally optimal because of prior processing, the benefit of annealing will be diminished.
